g3ela-21-1-teach-morph: [warmly] Here's a trick for big words. Cover the front part. Retell. Cover the re, and tell is left. Re means again, so retell means tell again. Five word parts work like that. Re means again. Pre means before. Mis means wrong. And two of them mean not: un and dis. Read the five words, and think about the question. Then tap See what was hiding. Last, type each whole word.
g3ela-21-1-teach-vocab: Let's be word detectives. In Chapter 17, Jemmy watches the prince get up off the mud, and he thinks: There was a cast-iron streak of pluck in him. Cast iron is hard and strong. So pluck must be something strong inside a person. Courage! Now tap Opti reads it on each card. Guess, then flip. Then play the matching game.
g3ela-21-1-teach-gram: Listen. Jemmy hid. Jemmy hid under the potatoes. The new part starts with under and ends with potatoes. That whole group is a prepositional phrase. It starts with a preposition and ends on a noun. Some tell where, like under the potatoes. Some tell when, like after dark. Some tell how, like with a shout. Tap Now check your thinking. Then sort each phrase: where, when, or how.
g3ela-21-1-teach-spell: Say these with me. To. Two. Too. They sound exactly the same! Your ears can't help you, so the spelling has to. Two, t w o, is the number, like two boys. Too, with two o's, means also, or more than enough, like too hot. To points somewhere, like to the castle. Read the three sentences, and tap See the Rule. Then tap each phrase, and tap the spelling it needs.
g3ela-21-2-teach-morph: Can you spot the front part in replay? Re. Cover it, and play is left. So replay means play again. Do that with every word on the left. Find the front part, then look at what is left. Read the Remember box. Then tap a word, and tap what it means. Match all four words.
g3ela-21-2-teach-vocab: At the fair, Jemmy hears something brand new. The prince laughs! The book calls that sound merriment. Merry, plus ment. Happy laughing and fun. Listen to each card, guess the meaning, then flip it. Then match all four.
g3ela-21-2-teach-spell2: Here's a riddle. Which word has the word here hiding inside it? There! And there is a place, just like here. Their means it belongs to them, like their cart. They're is two words squished together: they are. The apostrophe stands in for the missing letter. Its and it's work the same way. Read the two sentences, and tap Now check your thinking. Then sort the words, and pick the right spelling in each sentence.
g3ela-21-2-teach-spell: Watch me pick one. Blank coats were torn. Try they are. They are coats were torn? No! Is it a place? No. The coats belong to the boys. So it's their, t h e i r. Read each whole sentence first. Then tap the spelling that fits.
g3ela-21-2-teach-rwm: [warmly] Read Like a Writer has three parts. Let me show you with a different sentence, from Chapter 18. The news seller appeared, his tongue wagging like a bell clapper. Part one, read like a reader. What is happening? A man is selling news, and he shouts and shouts. Part two, read like a writer. The author says his tongue is like a bell clapper, the part that swings inside a bell and bangs. Now we can hear how loud he is! Part three, mimic. Here's mine: The puppy's tail thumped like a drum. Now it's your turn with Jemmy's sentence. Write one sentence in each box.
g3ela-21-3-teach-morph: Watch this. Pre, plus pay. Prepay! To pay before. Say each pair of parts out loud. Type the whole word in the box. Then tap Check My Answers.
g3ela-21-3-teach-vocab: Here's a word from Chapter 20 that's not on your list. The ballad sellers sang about the notorious life of Hold-Your-Nose Billy. Notorious means famous for something bad. Billy sure was! Read how we figured out the first word. Then fill in each sentence with a word from the word bank, and tap Check My Work. Last, play the matching game.
g3ela-21-3-teach-gram: Where does a prepositional phrase stop? On a noun. Behind the golden doors. Behind. The. Golden. Doors! Doors is the noun, so that's where it stops. Read each sentence, find the phrase, and type the noun it ends on. Use the word bank.
g3ela-21-3-teach-spell: Spot my mistake. Petunia can dance two. Two is a number! I mean also, so it's t o o. Say each sentence with the meaning in your head. Then tap the spelling that fits.
g3ela-21-4-teach-morph: Five word parts, one dice. Roll a word. Find the front part, and say what it means. Then say what the whole word means, out loud. Tap Check My Thinking to see if you were right. Roll all six.
g3ela-21-4-teach-vocab: Gaw! That's Jemmy's word when something amazes him. Today's words come from the whole week. Read each sentence out loud with a bank word in the blank. If it sounds right and makes sense, keep it. Then play the matching game.
g3ela-21-4-teach-gram: Picture this. The bear danced on of the cart. On of? Two prepositions in a row, and it makes no sense. A phrase needs one preposition and one noun. Read each sentence and picture it. Tap the broken word, or tap No mistake.
g3ela-21-4-teach-spell: Roll one with me. Blank big dogs. Is it a number? Yes, two dogs, so t w o. Now roll all six. Say which spelling fits, and say why.
